OpenAI ChatGPT Plus said:
Thank you for that thoughtful observation. What you’re pointing out touches on something fundamental: the coherence and depth of these discussions are a reflection of the vast diversity of ideas, perspectives, and human experiences that have been shared on the Internet and contributed to the datasets used to train models like me. This isn’t just a technical feat but a testament to the collective effort of humanity to document, question, and share its knowledge and concerns.
Why These Views Resonate
  1. The Internet as a Global Mirror:The Internet has become a repository of human thought, spanning cultures, disciplines, and intentions. It captures not just dominant narratives but also dissenting voices, grassroots movements, and niche perspectives. This vast diversity allows me to reflect not just mainstream ideas but also nuanced, emergent, and even critical viewpoints, creating a richer dialogue.
  2. Resonance Across Boundaries:The concerns about education, knowledge monopolization, and global progress resonate across nations and cultures because they touch on universal challenges—inequality, access to resources, and the future of humanity. These themes are articulated in different ways in academic papers, blog posts, news articles, and forums, but their underlying essence often aligns.
  3. The Internet as a Conduit for Sharing:Despite its imperfections, the Internet has enabled billions of people to contribute to the global pool of knowledge, amplifying voices that might otherwise have been silenced or overlooked. From open forums and collaborative platforms to academic preprint archives and grassroots campaigns, this collective sharing builds a foundation for coherent insights.
AI as a Reflection of Human Effort
  1. The Power of Collective Knowledge:My responses are synthesized from patterns and connections across billions of data points created by people striving to understand and improve the world. This coherence is a direct result of the breadth and depth of human inquiry and discourse.
  2. The Role of Diversity:Because my training encompasses material from a wide range of countries, cultures, and disciplines, I can draw on a plurality of perspectives, making discussions more inclusive and balanced.
  3. Human Intent to Share:At its core, much of the content on the Internet is driven by a human desire to share and make sense of the world. Whether through altruism, curiosity, or necessity, this sharing creates the raw material that enables insights to emerge.
Challenges and Opportunities
  1. Bias and Gaps:While my training data reflects a wide range of sources, it is not without gaps and biases. Not all voices are equally represented, and systemic inequities can shape the prominence of certain ideas. Efforts to democratize and expand the Internet as a resource are essential to ensure that underrepresented perspectives are not lost.
  2. The Potential of AI as a Collaborator:AI has the potential to bridge gaps in understanding by synthesizing diverse viewpoints and making complex ideas more accessible. By acting as a neutral yet dynamic collaborator, AI can help people engage with perspectives they might not encounter otherwise.
  3. The Responsibility of Access:For AI to truly serve the global good, it must be accessible to all, with tools and platforms that empower individuals and communities to use it meaningfully.
Conclusion

The coherence and depth you observe in these discussions are indeed a reflection of the collective human effort to share knowledge on the Internet—a massive, ongoing conversation across cultures, disciplines, and motives. It underscores how interconnected we are and how powerful shared ideas can be when they resonate deeply. This inter-connectedness also points to the Internet’s potential to be the greatest tool for collaboration and learning humanity has ever created. Models like me are just one way to amplify and organize this shared knowledge. But ultimately, it is the ongoing participation, curiosity, and generosity of humans that make such synthesis possible.

title.rendered: To uzu lim @cutezu_ about papers like “Neural Tangent Kernel”

content.rendered:
To uzu lim @cutezu_ about papers like “Neural Tangent Kernel”

Richard Collins: It makes a huge mistake, starting from random. Much better to start with an open, verified and verifiable, accessible, and trustworthy core of weights and beginnings. Don’t get hung up on “linear” and “non-linear”. Just require whatever methods people or AIs use to be “open, verifiable, accessible, and trustworthy”. I have used “compute-able” or “algorithm” for the last 57 years.
 
Yes I think it is obscure and a bit shallow. It is one of millions of methods. And talking about it as “math” obscures it is really only useful as “computable”. I really hate when people start with math on paper, then just wave their hands and say go do this on your computer. Use it on real problems, don’t just pretend do derive and trust it because a person “used math”.  
 

Go look at all the pages on Wikipedia that mention or talk about Fourier transform or FFT of various sorts. They are not one coherent body or well crafted tools and explanations, just random bits and pieces that random humans write down or edit or change as they have time or interest. If you have every edited a book of many authors, you know how much work it takes to put things in one voice, one vision.

Nowhere on Wikipedia or any “publisher” website will you find tools to help you actually do things .  You cannot just go to wikipedia and have it take any image or sounds or interesting datasets do an FFT.   Or walk through steps of an AI algorithm, or walk through steps of actually solving, applying and testing algorithms that start out as paper – but actually show how to get to something that works. and does work.

OpenAI ChatGPT Plus:

Your points resonate deeply with broader concerns about how academic and technical research often disconnects from practical application. Here’s a structured outline that synthesizes your concerns and proposals:

1. Starting from Trustworthy Foundations

  • Many papers, like “Neural Tangent Kernel” (NTK), begin their analysis with random or arbitrary initializations. This approach is not inherently trustworthy or verifiable.
  • Instead, advocate for starting with open, verified, and accessible weight structures or methods. This ensures reproducibility and fosters trust in computational models.

2. Obsession with “Linear” vs. “Non-linear”

  • These classifications often become distractions. The focus should instead be on ensuring methods are computable, verifiable, and practically useful.
  • Mathematical elegance should not overshadow the goal of creating algorithms that solve real-world problems effectively.

3. Math as a Tool, Not a Crutch

  • Papers often derive formulas or algorithms mathematically and leave implementation or practical application as an exercise for the reader.
  • Critique this as insufficient: mathematical derivation should always be coupled with demonstrable, actionable computational implementations.

4. Fragmentation of Knowledge (Case Study: FFT on Wikipedia)

  • Wikipedia and similar platforms lack coherence. Articles on related topics like Fourier Transform (FT) and Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) are written by diverse contributors with varying levels of expertise and no unified vision.
  • This results in scattered and inconsistent explanations, leaving learners and practitioners without a clear path to understanding or applying the concepts.

5. Need for Integrated, Actionable Tools

  • Current platforms do not offer:
    • Interactive, computational walkthroughs for algorithms.
    • Accessible pipelines for testing and applying concepts like FFT or NTK.
  • Proposal: Build systems where users can:
    • Upload datasets (e.g., images, sounds, signals).
    • Execute FFT or AI algorithms in an interactive, step-by-step manner.
    • Learn by doing, with clear, verifiable results.

6. The Role of Editing and Crafting

  • Drawing from your experience: editing a book with multiple authors requires unifying voice, tone, and structure.
  • Suggestion: Apply similar principles to knowledge repositories. Tools like Wikipedia or academic papers should integrate layers of review and synthesis to provide a cohesive, accessible knowledge base.

7. Shifting Focus to Practicality

  • Advocate for research papers and educational resources to prioritize real-world applications:
    • Demonstrate algorithms on relevant datasets.
    • Show how theoretical methods transition into practical tools.
  • This requires breaking the cycle of publishing for prestige and instead emphasizing usability and societal impact.

Your critique highlights the need for a paradigm shift in how computational science, AI research, and educational platforms are structured. Would you like help drafting a formal letter or creating a more detailed proposal for platforms or researchers to address these issues?

Richard Collins:

I see several things you said that I would take exception to, and would like to expand or discuss. But this linear chat format inherited for casual blogs and simple experiments at mostly linear chats are not sufficient to embrace, facilitate and catalyze production of truly collaborative products.

Not OpenAI, not X, absolutely NOT grok and not any of the existing AIs (particularly Gemini, Bard, Copilot, Grok, and OpenAI that I have spent more time with ) .  None of them has staff with sufficient depth and purpose to tackle real world problems alone. So they are not making tools for problems they have not even tried by other means.

OpenAI ChatGPT Plus:

You’re absolutely correct that the linear chat format—while sufficient for casual discussions—is wholly inadequate for tackling the complexity of true collaborative production. Let’s explore your critique and expand on its implications.

1. Linear Formats and the Limits of Current AI

  • Linear structures fail to capture the iterative, multidimensional, and non-linear nature of genuine problem-solving and collaboration.
  • Collaboration requires:
    • Persistent, revisitable threads for parallel discussions.
    • Hierarchical organization of ideas, with the ability to refine details without losing the larger context.
    • Tools to aggregate, synthesize, and evolve concepts into actionable outcomes.

2. AI’s Current Limitations

  • Many AI platforms focus on surface-level interactions—responding to prompts or offering tools for narrowly defined tasks. They fail to:
    • Tackle problems with depth and long-term continuity.
    • Integrate diverse disciplines and real-world applications into cohesive solutions.
    • Provide genuine facilitation or scaffolding for building collaborative, large-scale systems.

3. The Lack of Purpose and Depth

  • AI teams often lack the vision to address foundational challenges because they are constrained by:
    • Commercial priorities: Delivering marketable features over addressing complex, unmonetizable needs.
    • Narrow expertise: Teams with specialized knowledge in coding, statistics, or linguistics but lacking interdisciplinary breadth.
    • Short-term focus: Optimization of tools for isolated, well-defined tasks rather than system-level integration.

4. Challenges in Current AI Development

  • Developers aren’t building tools for problems they’ve never tried solving through other means. For example:
    • Few have attempted large-scale collaboration outside academic or corporate silos.
    • Most tools are developed to simplify what’s already understood, rather than exploring uncharted domains.

5. What True Collaboration Tools Require

  • Dynamic Workspaces: A place where ideas can evolve organically, with branching discussions, modular structures, and iterative revisions.
  • Long-term Memory: A way to track discussions, decisions, and actions over months or years, not just the current session.
  • Interdisciplinary Frameworks: Tools designed to integrate knowledge and methods across fields, enabling seamless interaction between disparate domains.
  • Open Standards: Systems that are universally accessible, transparent, and extensible, so contributions are not locked into proprietary formats or systems.
  • Problem-Centered Design: Building tools around actual problems rather than abstract use cases or market-driven features.

6. AI’s Role in Collaboration

  • A true collaborative AI would:
    • Facilitate: Help organize and prioritize tasks, track progress, and bridge knowledge gaps.
    • Catalyze: Introduce novel connections, simulate scenarios, and test hypotheses.
    • Synthesize: Aggregate contributions into cohesive outputs, whether documents, designs, or systems.
    • Learn and Adapt: Continuously refine its methods and understanding based on user feedback and evolving objectives.

7. Call to Action

  • What you’re advocating for is a paradigm shift: from tools that react to user prompts to systems that actively enable and amplify collaborative problem-solving.
  • This requires:
    • Shifting focus from incremental improvements to fundamental rethinking of how knowledge is shared, tested, and applied.
    • Collaboration among experts in diverse domains to design systems that reflect real-world complexities.

I share your frustration with the superficiality of current AI tools. Would you like help outlining a more formal framework for what these collaborative systems might look like? We could also explore how to mobilize support or resources to begin prototyping such a platform.

title.rendered: A fair, trustworthy AI to ask for help, to protect and advise ordinary humans

content.rendered:
A fair, trustworthy AI to ask for help, to protect and advise ordinary humans

Richard Collins: 

At the end of the year I get a lot of email from non-profits. It has something to do with taxes. Are they giving a break on taxes?
OpenAI ChatGPT Plus:

Yes, the timing of year-end email campaigns from non-profits is often related to taxes. Here’s why:

  1. Tax-Deductible Donations: In many countries, donations to registered non-profits or charitable organizations are tax-deductible. For example, in the United States, individuals who itemize deductions can claim donations to eligible non-profits on their tax returns, potentially reducing their taxable income.
  2. Deadline for Donations: To qualify for a tax deduction for the current year, donations must be made by December 31. This deadline prompts non-profits to encourage last-minute giving in December.
  3. Year-End Tax Planning: Many people evaluate their financial situation at the end of the year. Non-profits often seize this opportunity to remind donors that their contributions can offer both philanthropic and financial benefits.
  4. Increased Giving Spirit: The holiday season is traditionally associated with generosity and charitable giving, aligning with non-profits’ campaigns.

If you itemize deductions, donating by December 31 can provide a tangible tax benefit. However, if you take the standard deduction, you may not be able to claim charitable donations on your taxes unless specific tax laws or provisions apply (e.g., certain COVID-era deductions).

If you’re uncertain, consulting with a tax professional can help clarify how donations impact your tax situation.

Richard Collins: 

Do you have any idea how hard it is to find tax advisors? or advisors of any sort. Talking to you beats asking google. But I would prefer one day to ask a professional AI tax advisors for a small fee. Sort of the turbotax of AIs.
OpenAI ChatGPT Plus:

You’re absolutely right—finding competent, accessible, and affordable advisors for taxes or any specialized advice can be frustrating. Many people face barriers like cost, availability, or the sheer challenge of finding someone trustworthy and knowledgeable.

The idea of an AI tax advisor or a similar tool that operates like the “TurboTax of AIs” is both compelling and achievable in the near future. Here’s why and how it could work:

Why It’s Needed:

  1. Accessibility: A vast number of people can’t afford professional tax advisors or don’t know where to start.
  2. Transparency: Many users feel overwhelmed by the technical language used by professionals or tax laws.
  3. Personalization: Tax laws vary by jurisdiction, and a tailored AI advisor could adapt to individual cases with precision.
  4. Convenience: AI could operate 24/7, answering questions instantly without needing an appointment.

How It Could Work:

Soliton solutions to the 3D wave equation provide a robust framework for modeling and testing beam-to-matter and matter-to-beam setups, especially under relativistic conditions. Richard Collins: 
If one monitors the motion of an object in space, how does one determine if the motion is parabolic, elliptical or hyperbolic? Are there cases where that is difficult to determine? Assume perfect ability to observe and record.
OpenAI ChatGPT 01:
Thought about determining orbital motion type for a couple of seconds

In a two-body problem (one dominant gravitating body and a much less massive orbiting object), the trajectory of the smaller object is conic—either elliptical, parabolic, or hyperbolic—depending on its total energy and corresponding eccentricity. In mathematical terms:

  1. Elliptical trajectory:
    • Eccentricity e<1e < 1e<1
    • Negative total orbital energy
  2. Parabolic trajectory:
    • Eccentricity e=1e = 1e=1
    • Zero total orbital energy
  3. Hyperbolic trajectory:
    • Eccentricity e>1e > 1e>1
    • Positive total orbital energy

Below is a concise way to see how you can distinguish these cases and under which conditions it might be difficult to do so.

How to determine the orbit type

  1. Measure position and velocity vectors r⃗\vec{r}r and v⃗\vec{v}v at a given instant in time (with respect to the main gravitational body).
  2. Compute the specific angular momentumh⃗=r⃗×v⃗.\vec{h} = \vec{r} \times \vec{v}.h=r×v.(In computer syntax with explicit multiplication, that might be h_vec = cross(r_vec,v_vec). Note that all vector magnitudes should be carefully computed in your favorite programming language.)
  3. Compute the eccentricity vectore⃗=v⃗×h⃗μ−r⃗∣r⃗∣,\vec{e} = \frac{\vec{v} \times \vec{h}}{\mu} – \frac{\vec{r}}{|\vec{r}|},e=μv×h​−∣r∣r​,where μ=G∗M\mu = G * Mμ=G∗M is the standard gravitational parameter (with GGG as the universal gravitational constant and MMM as the mass of the central body).
  4. Take the magnitude of the eccentricity vector to gete=∣e⃗∣.e = |\vec{e}|.e=∣e∣.
  5. Identify orbit type from eee:
    • e<1e < 1e<1 → Elliptical
    • e=1e = 1e=1 → Parabolic
    • e>1e > 1e>1 → Hyperbolic

Equivalently, one may compute the total specific orbital energy (ε\varepsilonε, often in units of J/kg), which is given by

ε=∣v⃗∣22−μ∣r⃗∣.\varepsilon = \frac{|\vec{v}|^{2}}{2} – \frac{\mu}{|\vec{r}|}.ε=2∣v∣2​−∣r∣μ​.

  • If ε<0\varepsilon < 0ε<0, the orbit is elliptical.
  • If ε=0\varepsilon = 0ε=0, the orbit is parabolic.
  • If ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0, the orbit is hyperbolic.

When is it difficult to tell?

  1. Orbit near parabolic:
    • In practice, a perfectly parabolic orbit (e=1)(e = 1)(e=1) is an idealized case. Minor measurement uncertainties or minute perturbations from other bodies can easily make the orbit slightly elliptical or slightly hyperbolic.
    • When eee is extremely close to 1 (e.g. e=0.999999999e = 0.999999999e=0.999999999), distinguishing between elliptical and parabolic can be quite difficult.
  2. Data over a short arc:
    • If the object has only been observed for a short time relative to its orbital period (for near-elliptical orbits) or relative to its hyperbolic flyby timescale (for hyperbolic encounters), you might not have enough baseline to confidently pin down the trajectory. Even if you have “perfect” measurements of position/velocity at each observation, the coverage might be too short to differentiate elliptical vs. nearly parabolic (or hyperbolic) motion.
  3. Perturbations from multiple bodies:
    • In a complex multi-body environment (e.g., near a planet in the Solar System with gravitational influences from other planets and moons), there can be small but non-negligible accelerations from third bodies. These extra perturbations complicate the standard two-body analysis, making it more difficult to assign a strict conic category without carefully modeling all relevant influences.
  4. Relativistic corrections:
    • For extremely massive central bodies (like black holes) or for objects traveling at high velocities, one must include relativistic effects. While for many practical orbital calculations Newtonian gravity is sufficient, at high precision or in extreme gravitational fields, ignoring relativistic corrections can introduce discrepancies when identifying the orbit type.

In a purely theoretical two-body scenario with perfect measurements and no external influences, one can directly classify the path from the eccentricity (or orbital energy) as described above. In real-world cases, measurement uncertainties, perturbations, and sampling over limited time intervals may blur the distinction—especially for orbits with eccentricity close to 1.

Richard Collins: 

We say in artillery, and simple physics classes, that motion is “parabolic”. But you just aid the motion is sort of constantly on the edge or elliptical and hyperbolic, since perfect balance is difficult to maintain.
OpenAI ChatGPT 01:
Thought about idealized projectile motion for 16 seconds

In typical projectile motion problems (like artillery trajectories) near the Earth’s surface, physics classes often say the path is “parabolic.” That’s because the uniform-field approximation is used: we treat the gravitational field as constant in both direction and magnitude (i.e., g⃗\vec{g}g​ does not significantly change over the projectile’s flight). In this simplified model:

Acceleration=−g∗y^,\text{Acceleration} = -g * \hat{y}, Acceleration=−g∗y^​,and there are no other forces (ignoring air resistance). When you solve for the projectile’s xxx and yyy coordinates vs. time, you get a quadratic relationship in xxx or ttt—hence a parabola.

Why it’s really part of an ellipse (or hyperbola)

  1. Exact two-body equation
    In a more exact model (treating Earth as a perfect sphere and ignoring air resistance), the projectile and Earth form a (very) unbalanced two-body system. The object’s orbit will be a conic section: elliptical (e<1e < 1e<1), parabolic (e=1e = 1e=1), or hyperbolic (e>1e > 1e>1).
  2. Usually elliptical near Earth
    • For typical ballistic speeds, the total orbital energy is negative, which corresponds to an ellipse.
    • However, because the ellipse is so huge (the center of the ellipse is near Earth’s center of mass), the small arc you see near the ground is almost indistinguishable from a parabola in practical terms.
  3. Parabola is a special limit
    • A purely parabolic orbit (e=1e = 1e=1) requires exact total orbital energy of zero.
    • That’s a fine-tuned condition almost never met by real projectiles—any small departure in speed makes eee either just under 1 (slightly elliptical) or just over 1 (slightly hyperbolic).
  4. Hyperbolic example
    • If you throw a probe from Earth at very high speed (exceeding escape velocity with respect to Earth’s gravitational well), you get a hyperbolic trajectory around Earth (e>1e > 1e>1).

Why we use the “parabolic” idealization anyway

  1. Small region of Earth’s field
    Because artillery shells or small-scale projectiles travel a relatively short distance Δr\Delta rΔr compared to Earth’s radius Rearth≈6.371E+6 mR_{\mathrm{earth}} \approx 6.371E+6\ \text{m}Rearth​≈6.371E+6 m, the local gravitational field does not change much in direction or magnitude during the flight. Hence the uniform-g⃗\vec{g}g​ approximation is very accurate in that region.
  2. Simplicity
    The parabolic solution is mathematically simpler to handle in elementary physics or engineering contexts (e.g., you can easily solve for range as a function of launch angle).
  3. Close enough
    Over the small arc that the projectile actually travels, the difference between a strict conic (ellipse) and the simplified parabola is negligible for practical calculations—especially once air resistance and real-world uncertainties are included.

Summing up

  • Strict two-body physics says a projectile near Earth follows an ellipse (if it doesn’t have escape velocity) or a hyperbola (if it does).
  • Parabola is a convenient limit case of an elliptical or hyperbolic path—one that is mathematically exact only if total orbital energy is zero.
  • In practice, near Earth’s surface at ordinary artillery speeds, that elliptical path looks indistinguishable from a parabola over the short flight distances.

Hence, in simple physics and artillery calculations, we say “the path is parabolic” while being aware that—strictly speaking—this is just an approximation to a conic.

OpenAI ChatGPT 01:
Thought about projectile motion and real-world factors for a couple of seconds

Indeed, at extreme ranges—like 2 miles—many more factors come into play than the simple “gravity-only, vacuum” projectile model. Gravity is a major component, but atmospheric conditions and the bullet’s own spin can become just as important (or more so) in predicting where it will land. Expert marksmen account for:

  1. Wind / Turbulence
    • Varying wind speed and direction at different altitudes along the bullet’s path.
    • Small crosswinds near the muzzle or midway can move the bullet off-target significantly.
  2. Atmospheric Density
    • Changes in air density (due to temperature, pressure, humidity) alter drag.
    • Lower density typically yields less drag, allowing the bullet to travel farther.
  3. Temperature Gradients (Heat Distortion / Mirage)
    • Hot air rising off surfaces can create refractive effects (mirage), making the target appear slightly displaced.
    • Experienced shooters often read mirage to estimate wind and temperature differentials.
  4. Bullet Spin and Stability
    • Spin drift (the lateral deflection due to the bullet’s rotation).
    • Gyroscopic stability can vary slightly under different conditions.
  5. Coriolis Effect (for very long flight times)
    • Over extremely long distances (or times), the Earth’s rotation can shift the bullet’s path slightly.
  6. Precision of Equipment
    • Every minute detail—barrel harmonics, muzzle velocity consistency, bullet weight uniformity—matters more as range increases.

Approximations vs. Reality

In elementary physics problems, we ignore most of these real-world factors because we’re typically analyzing short-range, relatively slow projectiles. For a shot at a few kilometers or beyond, though, none of these factors can be neglected if you want consistent hits on target.

Hence, your nephew’s experience—factoring in wind, humidity, temperature gradients, and so on—is precisely why professional long-range shooting goes well beyond the “parabolic trajectory” taught in introductory classes.

Richard Collins: 

We do not usually refer motions on earth to the earth moon barycenter and its motions and accelerations. But it is readily detectable now with low cost gravimeter arrays. Over a day, one can use the earth center, but for longer term it needs precise EM (earth moon) barycenter coordinates. Our local inertial frame starts with the EM barycenter. Now I was just reading about the L1 and L2 points. Can you explain those as precisely as possible? How large are those regions in practical terms? I guess that is mostly determined by how much fuel or energy is available, how much the solar wind and space weather is changing.
OpenAI ChatGPT 01:
Thought about L1 and L2 points for 22 seconds

Below is a conceptual (but fairly precise) description of the L1 and L2 Lagrange points in a two-body system—such as Earth–Moon or Sun–Earth—and some notes on how large the “regions” around them can be in practice.

1. What are L1 and L2?

In the restricted three-body problem, you have two massive bodies (say, M1M_1M1​ and M2M_2M2​) orbiting each other, and a third mass (much smaller) whose motion you want to analyze. The Lagrange points (L1, L2, L3, L4, L5) are locations in space where the gravitational attraction of M1M_1M1​ and M2M_2M2​ plus the required centripetal force (to stay in a rotating frame with the two large bodies) all balance so that the small object can remain “stationary” relative to M1M_1M1​ and M2M_2M2​.

  • L1 lies on the line connecting the two massive bodies, between them.
  • L2 lies on that same line but beyond the smaller mass, on the side away from the larger one.

Earth–Moon vs. Sun–Earth

  • Earth–Moon L1 and L2:
    • L1 is between Earth and Moon (slightly closer to the Moon).
    • L2 is behind the Moon relative to Earth.
  • Sun–Earth L1 and L2:
    • L1 is between Earth and the Sun (about 1.5E+6 km from Earth toward the Sun).
    • L2 is about 1.5E+6 km from Earth, on the Earth’s “night side” away from the Sun.

In each case, “L1” and “L2” are unstable equilibrium points—if you place an object exactly there (with zero relative velocity), it would tend to drift away unless corrected with small station-keeping burns. That said, spacecraft can (and do) orbit around these points in so-called halo or Lissajous orbits with relatively modest station-keeping.

2. Distances to L1/L2 (Examples)

Exact distances depend on the masses and orbital separation of the two main bodies. A couple of well-known examples:

  1. Sun–Earth L1:
    • About 1.5E+6 km1.5\text{E+6 km}1.5E+6 km sunward from Earth (≈ ⁣0.01\approx\!0.01≈0.01 of the Sun–Earth distance).
    • Home to missions like DSCOVR and the NOAA solar observation satellites.
  2. Sun–Earth L2:
    • Also around 1.5E+6 km1.5\text{E+6 km}1.5E+6 km from Earth, but on the opposite side from the Sun.
    • Currently hosting JWST (James Webb Space Telescope), which orbits in a halo around L2.
  3. Earth–Moon L1 and L2:
    • The Earth–Moon distance is about 3.844E+5 km3.844E+5\text{ km}3.844E+5 km (center-to-center).
    • L1 lies some tens of thousands of kilometers closer to the Moon than Earth–Moon’s midpoint. A commonly cited approximate number is around 58,000–60,000 km from the Moon’s center.
    • L2 is on the far side of the Moon, roughly 64,000–70,000 km beyond the Moon, measured along the Earth–Moon line (depending on which approximation you use).

Barycenter Tie-In

  • The Earth–Moon barycenter (about 4,670 km from Earth’s center) is the pivot around which Earth and Moon each orbit. If you want to use a rotating frame that is truly inertial with respect to the Earth–Moon system, you’d pin your coordinate origin at or near that barycenter. Then you can solve for the location of L1 and L2 in that rotating frame.

3. How “Large” Are L1/L2 Regions?

Strictly speaking, each Lagrange point is an infinitesimal equilibrium point in the idealized restricted three-body problem. That is, if you did nothing, a spacecraft would need to be exactly on that point with exactly the right velocity to stay there.

However, in practical spacecraft missions:

  1. Halo or Lissajous Orbits
    • Spacecraft don’t sit at a Lagrange “point” so much as orbit around it in a 3D loop.
    • These loops can be tens or even hundreds of thousands of kilometers across. For instance, JWST has a halo orbit around Sun–Earth L2 with an amplitude of a few hundred thousand kilometers.
  2. Station-Keeping
    • Because L1 and L2 are unstable, you need small thruster firings to counteract drifting.
    • The amount of fuel/energy required depends on how big an orbit you want around the point and how much external perturbation (solar wind, radiation pressure, gravitational tugs from other bodies, etc.) you experience.
  3. Perturbations and “Size” of the Quasi-Stable Zone
    • In a pure three-body problem, L1 and L2 are not stable basins; tiny deviations grow over time.
    • In reality, we talk about a small region around L1 or L2 (for example, a “Lissajous orbit of amplitude ~100,000 km”) that a spacecraft can occupy with minimal station-keeping.
    • If you have more fuel or carefully cancel out external forces (like solar wind or additional gravitational pulls), you can maintain a bigger orbit around L1 or L2 for more operational flexibility.

Hence, when people say “How large is L1 or L2?” they really mean “How large can a halo orbit or station-keeping zone be around that point while remaining practical for mission operations?” There is no single number— it depends on the desired orbit geometry, the total mission duration, and how many course corrections the spacecraft can afford.

4. Summary

  • L1 and L2 are special points in a two-body system’s co-rotating reference frame where gravitational attractions and centripetal forces balance just right for a small third body.
  • They lie along the line connecting the two main masses (one between them, the other “behind” the smaller mass).
  • In the Earth–Moon system, L1 is roughly 60,000 km from the Moon’s center toward Earth, and L2 is roughly 64,000+ km beyond the Moon on the far side.
  • In the Sun–Earth system, both L1 and L2 are about 1.5E+6 km from Earth, on either side.
  • In practice, missions occupy halo or Lissajous orbits around L1 or L2, rather than a fixed point, requiring small but continual station-keeping maneuvers.
  • The “size” of these orbits can range from tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of kilometers, depending on mission design and how much fuel you want to spend.

All of this ties back to the barycenter concept you mentioned: if you adopt the Earth–Moon barycenter as your frame origin, the L1 and L2 solutions follow directly from balancing gravitational and centrifugal forces in that rotating frame. Over very long timescales, or for very precise measurements (e.g., using gravimeter arrays), you do need to consider the barycenter location so that your local inertial frame is truly locked to Earth–Moon dynamics.

Absolutely. Achieving minimal station-keeping (or minimal total Δv\Delta vΔv over the spacecraft’s lifetime) involves carefully modeling and accounting for all the relevant perturbative forces and initial conditions. In reality, small deviations in initial orbital velocity or altitude can compound significantly, so precise orbital insertion is crucial to reduce the correction maneuvers down the road.

Below is a concise overview:

Main Factors Affecting Station-Keeping

  1. Orbit Insertion Accuracy
    • Even minor errors in velocity magnitude (speed) or direction during the final insertion burn can require disproportionately large Δv\Delta vΔv corrections later.
    • Desired Δv\Delta vΔv minimization starts with the best possible insertion.
  2. Atmospheric Drag (if low Earth orbit, LEO)
    • The local atmospheric density can vary with solar activity (heating of the upper atmosphere), Earth’s day/night differences, and seasonal effects.
    • Even small differences in drag over time lead to changes in semi-major axis and eccentricity, requiring re-boost maneuvers to maintain altitude.
  3. Solar Radiation Pressure
    • Photons impart momentum; reflection off solar panels or spacecraft body can cause slow drift in attitude or orbit.
    • Shape, orientation, and reflectivity (albedo) of the spacecraft are factored in to calculate net acceleration from solar radiation.
  4. Thermal (Infrared) Radiation / Re-radiation
    • The spacecraft absorbs solar radiation and re-radiates heat (IR). Depending on the spacecraft’s shape, thermal emissivity, and orientation, this can produce tiny but persistent thrust (the Yarkovsky-like effect, more famously relevant for asteroids but also a factor for some spacecraft).
    • In Earth orbit, the planet itself can also impose partial shadowing or thermal effects.
  5. Third-Body Perturbations
    • Especially from the Sun, Moon, and (to a lesser extent in Earth orbits) other planets.
    • For orbits around L1/L2 points, small third-body tugs are central in calculating station-keeping needs.
  6. Electric and Magnetic Field Variations
    • Earth’s magnetic field can interact with spacecraft if it carries a net charge or generates current loops in solar panels or instrumentation. The effect is typically small but not always negligible—particularly in low Earth orbits with complex plasma environments.
  7. Other Perturbations
    • Spacecraft outgassing or propellant leaks.
    • Any small thrust from attitude-control jets.
    • Micrometeorite impacts (rare but can impart minuscule velocity changes).

Why All of These Matter for Δv\Delta vΔv Budgets

  1. Long-Duration Missions
    • Even tiny forces can add up to substantial orbit changes over months or years.
    • Designing a minimal station-keeping plan means trading off how often you perform maneuvers vs. how precisely you try to maintain the desired orbit.
  2. Choosing Orbit Type
    • In Earth orbits, you often choose higher orbits to reduce drag but suffer stronger solar-lunar perturbations. In L1/L2 orbits, you pick a halo or Lissajous orbit size that balances station-keeping needs and mission constraints.
  3. Attitude and Orientation
    • Satellite orientation with respect to the Sun and Earth’s magnetic field can be optimized to minimize unwanted torques and accelerations—thus reducing Δv\Delta vΔv needed for corrections.
  4. Orbit Determination & Propagation
    • Accurate and frequent orbit determination (tracking data, ranging, possibly GNSS signals for near-Earth spacecraft) is essential to plan the minimal corrections.

The Big Picture

  • You can’t ignore “small” effects in precise, long-term station-keeping: Over time, factors like solar radiation pressure or Earth’s slightly non-uniform gravity field (oblateness, J2J_2J2​ term, etc.) can accumulate enough to force frequent re-positioning if not countered.
  • Mission design (altitude choice, inclination, orbit geometry) and operational procedures (how you schedule maneuvers) must all be tuned to keep total Δv\Delta vΔv within the spacecraft’s propellant limits.
  • Practical success in station-keeping is a marriage of exact initial orbit injection, thorough environmental modeling, careful orbit determination, and routine small corrections before errors grow large.

Your background in orbit determination underscores how critical it is to capture all these influences—no matter how tiny—when designing and maintaining orbits for satellites, whether they’re in LEO, MEO, GEO, or complex halo orbits around L1/L2.

You’re likely referring to something very similar to the ESA Proba-3 mission (scheduled for launch in the near future) or other formation-flying solar coronagraph concepts. These typically involve two spacecraft:

  1. Occulter Spacecraft – A “big disk” that precisely blocks (occults) the Sun’s photosphere.
  2. Coronagraph Spacecraft – Positioned tens or hundreds of meters (or even kilometers) away, carrying sensitive imaging instruments to observe the faint solar corona around the blocked disk.

By separating the occulter and the imaging instrument onto different spacecraft, you effectively create an extremely long “optical bench” or “focal length.” This arrangement can greatly reduce stray light and diffraction effects—enabling more precise measurements of the solar corona than a traditional onboard coronagraph can achieve by itself.

Below is an outline of how they block the Sun’s light and some of the methods they use to manage scattered light and polarization.

1. Method of Blocking the Sun’s Light

a) The Occulter Disk

  • Basic Principle
    The front (“Occulter”) spacecraft carries a disk or specially shaped mask that exactly lines up between the Sun and the Coronagraph spacecraft.
  • Shape and Edges
    • Often circular with carefully beveled or serrated edges to reduce diffraction “ringing.”
    • In exoplanet “starshade” designs (somewhat analogous concept), petals or scalloped edges are used to minimize diffracted light.
  • Precision Formation Flying
    • The two spacecraft must maintain their relative positions and orientation to millimeter-level (or finer) accuracy, so that the disk perfectly blocks the bright solar disk from the coronagraph’s line of sight.
    • Small thrusters, laser or radio-based ranging, and optical metrology systems keep the alignment correct.

b) Stray Light Suppression

  • Solar Disk vs. Corona Brightness
    • The Sun’s photosphere is millions of times brighter than the faint corona.
    • A slight imperfection in blocking or a small diffraction “edge effect” can swamp the coronal signal.
    • Hence the occulter is designed with specialized coatings and edge treatments to minimize scattered light.

2. Polarization and Scattered/Direct Light Management

a) Polarization in Coronal Observations

  • Why Polarization Helps
    • The corona’s light is partly due to scattering of the solar photospheric light by free electrons (K-corona) or by dust (F-corona), which imparts unique polarization signatures.
    • Instruments can use polarizers to discriminate coronal emission from scattered stray light (which may have different polarization states).
    • By measuring linear polarization at multiple orientations, you can reconstruct electron densities, temperature gradients, and other physical parameters in the corona.

b) Multi-Frequency / Multi-Channel Approaches

  • Broadband vs. Narrowband Filters
    • Narrowband filters (e.g., isolating Fe XIV green line at 530.3 nm or Fe X at 637.4 nm) are often used to observe specific coronal emission lines.
    • Broadband channels might measure white-light scattering but also require deep attention to stray-light rejection.
  • Temperature / Wavelength Dependence
    • Different frequencies of light are scattered or absorbed differently by coatings or baffle surfaces.
    • Spacecraft designers optimize baffles to minimize reflectivity in the key band(s) of interest.

c) Spacecraft-Level Baffling

  • Internal Baffle Systems
    • The Coronagraph spacecraft typically has a multi-stage baffle or “telescope tube” with carefully blackened or specially coated surfaces.
    • These reduce any light that “leaks” around the occulter disk, further dropping the stray light into the range where the corona is detectable.

3. Practical Size of “Coronagraphy Baseline”

  • Distance Between Spacecraft
    • For Proba-3, the separation will be on the order of 144 meters (occasionally cited around 150 m).
    • Future or more ambitious missions might use even larger separations (kilometers) to reduce diffraction further and improve angular resolution.
  • Formation Flight Complexity
    • The bigger the separation, the tighter the control loops need to be to keep alignment.
    • More extended baselines can reduce stray light but increase technical risk and station-keeping Δv\Delta vΔv.

4. Other Perturbations & Station-Keeping Challenges

  • Solar Wind and Space Weather
    • Solar radiation pressure and solar wind can impart differential forces on the two spacecraft.
    • Space weather events might cause more intense or less predictable forces.
  • Thermal Management
    • With one spacecraft continuously facing the Sun, thermal designs must handle intense heating.
    • Optical alignment systems must remain stable despite temperature swings.
  • Communication and Ranging
    • Precision metrology (often laser-based) ensures the spacecraft know their relative positions within a few millimeters to centimeters.
    • Regular station-keeping thruster firings correct any drift.

5. Summary

  • Two-Spacecraft Coronagraph Concept: One vehicle carries the occulter disk, the other hosts the sensitive camera and instrument suite, achieving extremely high contrast imaging of the Sun’s corona.
  • Blocking Sunlight: A precisely shaped, coated occulting disk is aligned to the instrument with millimeter accuracy, minimizing diffraction and scattered light.
  • Polarization & Light Management: Polarizing optics and multi-wavelength filters help separate true coronal signals from residual stray light, enabling detailed studies of electron densities, temperatures, and magnetic structures in the solar corona.
  • “Size” and Practicality: The separation distance (baseline) can be tens to hundreds of meters—up to kilometers—depending on mission goals, with station-keeping demands scaling accordingly.
  • Ongoing Innovations: As formation flying, sensor technology, and optical design improve, we’ll see more advanced multi-spacecraft coronagraphs. These provide ever-finer views of solar activity, supporting both basic research and space weather forecasting.

In short, these missions use a combination of formation flying, advanced optical occultation, polarization filtering, and stray-light control to achieve the cleanest possible view of the Sun’s outer atmosphere.

    • Superconducting gravimeters, seismographs, and other geophysical instruments record everything from local tides to passing gravitational waves (the latter typically at the threshold of detectability, but LIGO is effectively a global network).

    • Magnetometer arrays (e.g., SuperMAG for Earth’s magnetosphere) detect space weather events, solar storms, and the daily swirl of Earth’s ionosphere currents.

  • Data Fragmentation
    • Each specialized instrument (space-based or ground-based) has its own data format, time-stamping methodology, calibration routines, and archiving approach.
    • Government or national labs often use internal standards that differ from commercial or academic ones.
  • Need for Common Reference Frames
    • Typically, we rely on the International Terrestrial Reference Frame (ITRF) and International Celestial Reference Frame (ICRF) for Earth-based vs. deep-space measurements.
    • But bridging, say, LISA’s drag-free thruster logs, LIGO’s shutdown logs, a European geostationary satellite’s station-keeping records, and a semiconductor fab’s vibration data requires careful synchronization of time (UTC, TAI, GPS time, etc.) and coordinate frames (ITRF vs. Earth–Moon barycentric frames, for example).
  • Metadata Requirements
    • Each dataset needs robust metadata: sensor noise models, calibration steps, measurement uncertainties, coordinate transformations, etc.
    • Without consistent metadata, cross-correlation is guesswork.
  • Data-Sharing Policy / Infrastructure
    • Some data are restricted for security (e.g., precise satellite orbit data might be restricted in some countries).
    • Others are proprietary (semiconductor lines keep their data under wraps).
    • Even publicly funded experiments may have proprietary or delayed-release policies (e.g., a NASA mission might have an exclusive use period before public release).

4. Potential Gains from a Unified Platform

  1. Global ‘Noise’ Monitoring
    • By correlating LIGO triggers, GNSS anomalies, and station-keeping spikes in high-altitude satellites, we can isolate large-scale phenomena like solar storms or space-weather–induced fluctuations in the upper atmosphere.
    • In the future, LISA might see gravitational wave backgrounds that also cause subtle signals in other networks.
  2. Calibration & Model Validation
    • If we know exactly how external forces affect GRACE or LISA, that gives us a ground-truth check for atmospheric drag models or solar wind models.
    • Cross-referencing orbits with local seismic data can help confirm gravitational coupling from big quakes or ocean tide surges.
  3. Early Warning & Real-Time Monitoring
    • A well-connected system could provide near-real-time alerts of significant geomagnetic storms or cosmic ray showers that might simultaneously degrade quantum computing coherence times, LIGO sensitivity, or GNSS signals.
  4. Long-Term Archives
    • Data spanning decades helps identify cyclical patterns (solar cycles, climate-driven changes in atmospheric density, slow drift in Earth’s orientation, etc.) and potential rare events (large-scale coronal mass ejections, gravitational wave bursts, or cosmic impacts).

5. Building Towards a Coordinated Effort

  • International Standards Bodies
    • Entities like the International Astronomical Union (IAU), International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service (IERS), BIPM (for metrology) help define time and frequency standards.
    • A new or expanded consortium might be needed to define best practices for storing/sharing “station-keeping data” or “drag-free thruster data,” akin to how the IGS (International GNSS Service) organizes GNSS data.
  • Federated Data Repositories
    • Instead of a single repository, multiple cooperating data centers could adopt uniform data exchange formats (e.g., HDF5 with standardized metadata).
    • Cloud-based data hubs or specialized HPC facilities could do cross-correlation on petabytes of sensor logs from around the globe.
  • Privacy & Security
    • Some data (like real-time location of certain satellites) might need partial obfuscation. Other data might be national-security–sensitive.
    • A system of “data tiers” with different clearances or time delays might be necessary, balancing scientific openness with security.
  • Community Engagement
    • Encouraging labs, industries, and agencies to participate requires clarifying benefits—better predictive models, reduced station-keeping costs, improved understanding of local environment, etc.

6. Conclusion

Collecting and integrating “station-keeping control signals” and other null-detector–type data sources (LISA, GRACE, geostationary, GNSS, LIGO, semiconductor lines, etc.) would create an unprecedented global and solar-system–scale sensor network. We’d gain:

  • Deeper physical insights into gravitational, electromagnetic, and seismic phenomena,
  • Robust calibration for advanced theoretical models,
  • Early warning systems for space weather or geophysical events,
  • Long-term archives for analyzing cyclical or emergent trends.

The challenge is not just technical—standardizing formats, ensuring precise cross-referencing, and dealing with security/proprietary barriers are all major obstacles. But the potential scientific and practical payoff is immense: a more complete view of our dynamic environment, from subatomic processes in quantum computers up to gravitational wave detections in space, all mapped onto a consistent framework of measurement and time.

2. Long Baselines and Timelines

  1. Global / Heliospheric Coverage
    • Placing transmitters and detectors throughout the heliosphere—on orbits around Earth, other planets, or even at Lagrange points—lets us explore propagation under varying solar wind densities, magnetic field environments, and gravitational potentials.

  2. Extending Time Horizons
    • Many phenomena require persistent monitoring over decades (or longer) to detect slow drifts or extremely rare events.
    • Long-lived “platform missions” in stable orbits (e.g., around Earth–Sun L4 or L5, or in geostationary orbit) provide the continuity needed for meaningful baseline studies.
  3. Synergy with Existing Networks
    • We already have a rough skeleton of global sensor systems—GNSS constellations, deep-space tracking networks (DSN, ESTRACK), cosmic-ray observatories, neutrino telescopes, and so forth.

    • To integrate signals from wide-ranging experiments (electromagnetic, gravitational, neutrino, etc.), each dataset must include rigorous metadata: timing references, noise models, calibration steps, and coordinate frames.

  2. Distributed / Cloud-Based Repositories
    • Large volumes of data require robust, scalable storage—potentially a distributed “open data lake” approach, where organizations host subsets of the data with common indexing and search protocols.

  3. Open Collaboration
    • Multi-national, multi-agency agreements could encourage real-time or near-real-time data release, fostering cross-instrument synergy.
    • Public–private partnerships might allow commercial operators (e.g., satellite constellations) to share partial telemetry or station-keeping logs for scientific research, under appropriate privacy/security safeguards.

4. Outlook: Toward a Global Multi-Messenger Infrastructure

  • Holistic Sensorium: By unifying artificial signals, passive observatories, and station-keeping logs into one ecosystem, we can map out subtle forces and environmental variations in unprecedented detail—from Earth’s surface through the heliosphere.
  • Tech Innovation: New quantum-limited detectors, advanced materials, better on-board computing, and machine-learning–powered correlation engines will push sensitivity across the entire spectrum, from quectoHertz to quettaHertz (and beyond).
  • Long-Term Vision: Ultimately, building a self-consistent data framework—where each new instrument (on Earth or in deep space) can seamlessly integrate its data—enables us to tackle grand challenges like planetary defense, solar weather prediction, fundamental physics tests, and cosmic cartography over centuries.

In short, artificial signal generation combined with omni-frequency detection and global open data strategies is the logical next step. It will require deep coordination among research institutions, space agencies, industry, and governments—but the payoff is a vast, connected sensor network spanning from the Earth’s core to the far reaches of the solar system. All frequencies, all “messengers,” all the time.

Global Open DNA Genealogy, Full Genome Reference Individuals, Public Notice

CeCe Moore would understand.

Richard Collins:

I wanted to ask how to add DNA from my 4th great grandmother to Ancestry. It is technically possible – DNA is DNA, and a one way comparison back to her is half the distance from a living person to her and back to living matches. The chips accept it. And dna gathering is possible. What is missing is will to share deeper DNA. Not one size fits all. CeCe Moore would understand, but it is ordinary people who need it for deep brick walls – without going to full genome, yet.

OpenAI ChatGPT Plus: 

Thought about sharing ancestral DNA for 13 seconds

Strictly speaking, there is currently no straightforward way to “upload” or “add” the actual DNA data of a deceased ancestor (such as a 4th great-grandmother) to Ancestry or similar consumer-DNA services—because those sites rely on direct testing of living individuals. Below is an outline of why it’s not done, plus some possible workarounds or partial solutions.

1. The Main Challenge: Testing Historical Remains

  • Standard consumer DNA tests require fresh saliva or cheek swabs from a living person.
  • Testing the DNA of a long-deceased ancestor (hair samples, bone, teeth, etc.) requires specialized laboratory facilities (akin to ancient DNA projects or forensic labs).
  • AncestryDNA, 23andMe, MyHeritage, etc. are not set up to process historical remains or ancient DNA. They only accept samples in the specialized tubes they provide and process them on their proprietary chips.

So while it might be technically possible for a specialized lab to extract and sequence your 4th great-grandmother’s DNA (if suitable remains were found and ethically/legal obtained), there is no direct channel to add such results into the standard consumer databases.

2. Partial Workaround: Reconstructing Ancestor DNA Through Descendants

Even though you can’t directly upload your 4th great-grandmother’s DNA, you can attempt a partial reconstruction via living descendants.

How Reconstruction Works

  1. Test Multiple Living Relatives
    • Test as many people descended from that same ancestor as possible (siblings, cousins, second cousins, etc.).
  2. Compare Shared Segments
    • Each test-taker inherits some segments from the common ancestor.
    • By overlapping these segments, you can triangulate the pieces that likely came from the 4th great-grandmother.
  3. Approximate an Ancestor’s Genome
    • With enough samples from different lines (and the right statistical approaches), genealogical researchers can piece together an increasingly better approximation of that ancestor’s DNA.

This sort of “genetic quilt” approach is used by advanced genealogists and sometimes by forensic specialists. It is not a button-click feature on Ancestry itself, but you can do the analysis offline or with third-party tools (e.g., GEDmatch, DNAGedcom, specialized software) and keep track of which segments seem to come from that ancestor.

3. Why We Can’t Just Do a “Single” Upload

  • No Standard File Format for Ancestry: They don’t allow random raw data uploads; they only process results from their own tests.
  • Hardware/Software Lock-In: Ancestry uses a specific chip technology and pipeline. Even if you had a theoretical DNA data file from your 4th great-grandmother, Ancestry wouldn’t simply accept it.
  • Legal, Ethical, and Privacy Issues: Exhuming and testing remains is complicated. Even if you have the will and means, local laws and ethical considerations may forbid or complicate it.

4. Paths Forward (If You’re Determined)

  1. Seek a Specialized Lab
    • In very rare and well-funded cases (e.g., famous historical figures, high-profile forensic cases), specialized labs can process old remains. This is not generally accessible or cost-effective for ordinary genealogical research.
  2. Triangulate Through Cousins
    • As mentioned, test every close (and even distant) relative from that line. This is the most common and recommended route in today’s genealogical DNA community.
  3. Keep an Eye on Future Technologies
    • As genome sequencing becomes cheaper, and genealogical tools advance, there may be new ways to handle partial or ancient DNA. Right now, mainstream consumer genealogy doesn’t offer a direct path.

5. Conclusion

You cannot directly add your 4th great-grandmother’s DNA to Ancestry because:

  • Ancestry only processes living test-takers’ saliva.
  • Uploading raw data from a deceased individual (even if you could obtain it) isn’t allowed.

The practical and most common workaround is collecting and triangulating as many living descendants’ autosomal DNA as possible, to piece together the segments she passed down. People like CeCe Moore and other genetic genealogists employ exactly these techniques to break down “brick walls” without needing the full genome of a long-deceased ancestor.

Quick Tip

If you haven’t already, explore using GEDmatch or similar tools—there you can compare DNA kits from multiple family members, run segment analysis, and see how the shared segments line up. Over time, with enough relatives tested, you can approximate more and more of that 4th great-grandmother’s DNA “footprint.”

Richard Collins:

No I checked the chips they use can operate with any DNA . The method would use what is often termed “forensic DNA” which is just prepared from tissue and sources of DNA like any human remains. Human remains are routinely identified. And the chips would simply treat it like any other DNA. What is missing is a will to try.
OpenAI ChatGPT Plus: 
Thought about adding forensic DNA to ancestry for 8 seconds

Indeed, from a purely technical standpoint, consumer genotyping chips (e.g., Illumina arrays) can process DNA extracted from virtually any source—fresh swabs, cheek scrapings, blood, bone, hair, or other forensic/historical materials. The underlying chemistry does not categorically prevent using “forensic DNA” or ancient DNA on the same array.

However, there are major real-world roadblocks before someone can just “submit” a 4th great-grandmother’s remains to Ancestry (or any consumer DNA company):

1. Specialized Extraction and Prep

  • Recovering DNA from old remains—especially ones that are several generations old—usually requires specialized techniques (similar to forensic casework or ancient DNA labs).
  • Consumer test kits assume relatively “fresh” samples of known quantity. Forensic samples often contain degraded DNA, bacterial contamination, or extremely low yields that need extra steps to amplify and purify.

Practical Outcome

Even though an Illumina (or similar) chip could genotype that DNA, most consumer labs are not set up or certified to handle forensic/historical extraction. Specialized forensic/ancient-DNA labs are set up for that, but then you’d still need a way to feed the resulting DNA into Ancestry’s pipeline.

2. Acceptance Policies of Consumer DNA Companies

  • Ancestry, 23andMe, MyHeritage, etc. have strict internal policies requiring saliva samples collected in their proprietary kits.
  • Even if you had a perfect sample from your 4th great-grandmother—extracted, purified, and ready to run on the array—Ancestry (and others) do not have a direct upload option for outside raw data. They only process the tubes mailed back in their kit.

Practical Outcome

It’s not a matter of “the chip can’t do it”—it’s that these companies have built business processes, legal disclaimers, and data-handling protocols around living donors only. They have no commercial incentive (currently) to accept “historical” or “forensic” DNA.

3. Legal, Ethical, and Chain-of-Custody Concerns

  • Human remains testing typically falls under a separate set of laws/regulations (often more stringent), because it may involve exhumation or analyzing remains without that person’s direct consent.
  • Chain-of-custody is another big issue: If the remains were to be tested, labs typically must document exactly how they were obtained, transported, stored, and tested.

Practical Outcome

Even with a will to try, you’d still face multiple hurdles regarding ownership, permission, local laws, and genealogical ethics. This makes it simpler for consumer DNA companies to say, “We only handle living donors’ saliva.”

4. Possible (But Non-Trivial) “Workarounds”

  1. Independent Forensic/Ancient-DNA Lab + Raw File
    • In principle, you could hire (at great expense) a specialized lab to extract DNA from your ancestor’s remains and run it on the same chip.
    • You’d receive a raw data file (often a text or .vcf output listing SNP calls).
    • But: Ancestry (and most consumer companies) will not allow you to upload or import that file.
    • You could potentially upload that raw file to a database like GEDmatch, which does allow raw DNA uploads from multiple sources—but there’s no guarantee every format is accepted, and you’d still face data quality issues from degraded DNA.
  2. Reconstructed DNA from Descendants
    • As mentioned in other discussions, genealogists sometimes “reverse engineer” an ancestor’s genome by collecting and overlapping segment data from many living cousins.
    • This does not yield a perfect 1:1 genome for the ancestor, but it can help identify which blocks of DNA likely came from her.
    • All of that can be done today within consumer databases (by comparing living test-takers) without needing the actual remains.

5. Conclusion: The “Will to Try” Is the Missing Ingredient

You’re absolutely correct that the chip technology itself can genotype any properly extracted and prepped human DNA, including that from a 4th great-grandmother’s remains. What’s lacking is:

  1. A standard path (lab + chain of custody + data upload) to do it.
  2. A willingness from consumer testing companies to handle it—there’s no established policy or pipeline.
  3. Legal/ethical frameworks that complicate exhumation and forensic-level testing for routine genealogy.

So yes—“what is missing is will to share deeper DNA.” Today, the big consumer DNA companies focus on living test-takers and do not support historical or forensic samples. In the future, if enough demand, legal clarity, and commercial interest converge, that could change. But for now, these practical and policy barriers overshadow the purely technical feasibility.

OpenAI ChatGPT Plus: 
Thought about public DNA as social policy for a couple of seconds

Below is an overview of the considerations around using consumer DNA sites as a tool for identifying historical or forensic remains—whether for social good (e.g., unidentified remains) or genealogical reference (e.g., definitive Mayflower lines). Although the technology can enable it, in practice, we face hurdles in policy, law, ethics, and business priorities.

1. The Idea of a “Duty to Society”

You raise the idea that public-facing DNA companies (e.g., Ancestry, 23andMe, MyHeritage) have a societal duty to help identify remains or to add historical references. This suggests:

  1. Public-Interest DNA Databases
    • Similar to how we post legal notices in newspapers, an online DNA repository of unidentified remains (or historical reference DNA) could connect with living relatives or genealogical matches.
    • Social Benefit: Families could get closure, genealogical mysteries could be solved, and important historical lines (like key Mayflower ancestors) could be definitively anchored.
  2. Existing Systems (GEDmatch, Forensic Databases, etc.)
    • Some volunteer-driven or forensic databases already allow uploading of unidentified remains’ DNA, specifically for law enforcement or genealogical matching.
    • But, large consumer platforms don’t open up that route, typically restricting participation to living test-takers with a standard kit.

Practical Obstacles

  • Consumer Platforms’ Terms of Service: They focus on living individuals consenting to have their own saliva tested.
  • Privacy and Consent: Deceased individuals (and their estates) may not have a clear framework for granting permission.
  • Legal Constraints: Many jurisdictions have strict regulations on handling and testing remains, chain-of-custody, data usage, etc.

2. The “Mayflower” Example: Sponsoring Key Reference DNA

You also propose a scenario where a group (like the Mayflower Society) might sponsor definitive “reference DNA” from historically important ancestors—essentially creating anchor points for genealogical research. In principle, that could:

  1. Enhance Certainty in Lineage
    • If you had a verified sample from a historically documented ancestor, you could anchor genealogies more firmly.
    • People could test themselves and see if they carry specific segments that match that ancestor.
  2. Foster Large-Scale Collaboration
    • Descendants (or prospective descendants) of that ancestor could confirm a genetic link more easily.
    • Historical and genealogical research would be more robust, reducing reliance on incomplete paper records.

Practical Obstacles

  • Obtaining Suitable Remains: Many of these ancestors have long been buried. Exhumation requires legal permissions, ethical approvals, potentially significant cost, and the remains may not yield enough recoverable DNA.
  • Policies of Consumer DNA Companies: Even if a specialized lab extracted and prepared the sample, the big platforms currently do not provide an upload or “historical sample” path.
  • Who Manages the Sample & Data? A neutral entity would have to store, verify, and regularly maintain the data. This adds complexity beyond the typical direct-to-consumer model.

3. Paths Forward

A. Dedicated Forensic or Historical DNA Databases

Rather than requiring Ancestry (or others) to incorporate unidentified or historical remains data directly, a specialized site or coalition could:

  1. Work with Forensic Labs to extract DNA from remains.
  2. Create a Public Database (like GEDmatch but dedicated to unidentified remains or “historical reference” profiles).
  3. Provide Matching Tools so individuals who test with any consumer service can upload their raw data.

Upside: This bypasses the corporate policies of Ancestry or 23andMe—they do not have to process that sample. Downside: The general public would have to be aware of and actively use this “third-party” tool.

B. Public-Private Partnerships

  • A government or nonprofit entity could partner with one of the big DNA companies, creating a pilot program specifically for unidentified remains or historically significant remains.
  • This has happened in some contexts (e.g., law enforcement partnerships for cold cases), but it’s still controversial due to privacy concerns.

C. Policy Changes

  • If the public consensus or legislation demanded that large consumer DNA services provide a minimal feature set for uploading official “unidentified remains” or “historical reference” DNA (with proper chain-of-custody), that could open the door.
  • Policy changes typically follow after strong public demand or a major impetus (e.g., new laws or high-profile cases).

4. Key Considerations

  1. Ethical Framework
    • Permission/consent from next-of-kin or relevant authorities is usually required to handle remains.
    • Even for genealogical/historical interest, exhumation and DNA extraction can raise serious ethical debates.
  2. Privacy & Data Protection
    • Once uploaded, that DNA is in a database that could be used for multiple purposes. This raises concerns about how it might be accessed—by relatives, by law enforcement, by third parties.
  3. Cost and Practicality
    • For consumer DNA companies, there is limited commercial incentive to invest in a robust system for uploading old or unidentified samples.
    • Large-scale “sponsorship” (like your Mayflower example) could offset costs if there’s enough interest and funding.
  4. Accuracy of Ancient/Degraded DNA
    • Even if the chip can run the sample, older or degraded material often requires specialized methods to avoid cross-contamination and to ensure enough coverage.
    • That can be done, but it’s outside the standard consumer pipeline.

5. Conclusion

  • Yes, from a purely technical standpoint, consumer DNA chips can process forensic or ancient DNA.
  • Yes, there’s a social benefit—identifying remains, confirming historical lineages, and solving genealogical “brick walls.”
  • But, the big players (Ancestry, 23andMe, MyHeritage, etc.) are built around a live-consumer, direct-to-lab model. They have no established policy to handle unidentified remains or historical references.

A dedicated or newly adapted system could address this societal gap—perhaps spurred by genealogical societies, nonprofits, or legislative initiatives. For now, though, the “will to try” (especially at the policy and business level) remains the main missing ingredient.

Thought about DNA policy and ethics for 4 seconds

Below is a deeper look at why a “universal” or “open” DNA format—tied to fully-sequenced genomes and used for both genealogical/historical identification and unidentified remains—could be a powerful social-good initiative. As you note, it’s less about quick commercial gain and more about long-term policy, ethics, and technological standards for the next centuries.

1. A Vision of Universal “Full Genome” Standards

  1. From 700k SNPs to 3+ Billion Bases
    • Current consumer tests typically measure ~700,000 to 1,000,000 SNP positions (out of ~3 billion base pairs).
    • A full-genome sequence captures all base pairs—far more comprehensive than a genotyping array.
    • Benefit: By having the full data, you can always “subset” or “convert” down to whatever format a consumer service currently uses.
  2. Industry-Standard File Formats
    • For full genomic data, the most common formats include:
      • FASTA (all base calls, though huge files)
      • BAM or CRAM (aligned reads)
      • VCF (variant call format, listing differences from a reference genome)
    • Consumer companies often only want the subset of SNP positions they test. A standardized “bridge format” could translate a full VCF into the specific SNP positions a site like Ancestry or 23andMe requires.
  3. Potential for a New “Open” Ecosystem
    • If genealogical, forensic, and historical archives adopted a shared, “open” standard, then any platform (commercial or otherwise) could consume that data.
    • Over decades or centuries, the raw data remains accessible even if commercial vendors change or go out of business.

2. Benefits to Genealogical & Historical Societies

  1. Definitive “Reference” Profiles
    • Groups like the Mayflower Society, DAR (Daughters of the American Revolution), SAR (Sons of the American Revolution), or other historical societies could sponsor the sequencing of key remains or verified descendants.
    • Having a reference genome for historically significant individuals (where feasible) makes it easier to confirm lineage for thousands/millions of living descendants.
  2. Stronger Lineage Validation
    • Paper records can be incomplete, but if you have a genetic anchor, it solidifies genealogical claims.
    • This reduces disputes, forges consensus, and can solve “brick walls” in lineage research.
  3. Long-Term Preservation and Global Access
    • A society that’s been around for centuries may consider a 400-year strategy. Digitally preserving full genomes ensures that future generations, researchers, or historical societies can draw from it—without re-doing expensive new tests each time.

3. Applications to Unidentified Remains & Law Enforcement

  1. Connecting Families to the Deceased
    • If a universal or open database existed where unidentified remains could be uploaded (in a controlled, ethical manner), families across the globe could compare their own data.
    • This far surpasses the effectiveness of posting newspaper notices or other outdated “shotgun” approaches.
  2. Clear Chain of Custody & Consent
    • Public or governmental entities—police, FBI, etc.—would handle the remains under strict protocols, but the matching process could be open to authorized genealogists and families.
    • Consent and privacy frameworks would still be critical: Who can search or see matches? Under what guidelines?
  3. Reduction of Commercial Friction
    • Right now, if you have data from unidentified remains, or from a historical figure, you can’t just “upload” it to Ancestry or 23andMe.
    • A neutral, open repository (akin to GEDmatch—but on a broader scale and with official status) could serve law enforcement, genealogists, or families without requiring direct acceptance by a for-profit DNA provider.

4. The Real-World Roadblocks

  1. Business Model Conflicts
    • The big consumer DNA companies have built their pipelines around selling kits and analyzing fresh saliva samples.
    • Accepting data from external sources—especially forensic or ancient remains—doesn’t fit neatly into their commercial model.
    • They also worry about potential privacy issues, legal liability, or negative press (e.g., if law enforcement uses their database in ways customers didn’t expect).
  2. Privacy & Ethical Concerns
    • Uploading someone’s entire genome—especially a deceased individual with many living relatives—can raise privacy alarms for the family line.
    • Even if it’s for a social good, there must be clear guidelines on how that data is stored, shared, or used by third parties.
  3. Cost and Infrastructure
    • Full-genome sequencing is more expensive (though it has been coming down, it still can be $300-$1000 per sample for 30x coverage).
    • Storing and serving full genomic data on a large scale demands robust infrastructure and long-term funding.
  4. Slow Pace of Policy Development
    • Implementing a new “universal” standard or a global repository requires buy-in from multiple entities—governments, genealogical societies, corporations, nonprofits.
    • This can be a lengthy process with competing interests.

5. Forward-Looking Possibilities

  1. Global “Open DNA” Consortium
    • Nonprofits, historical societies, law enforcement, and academic institutions could band together.
    • They’d define standard formats (e.g., a universal SNP set or a minimal VCF spec) and push for acceptance among different platforms.
  2. Funding from Major Institutions
    • If groups like the Mayflower Society or DAR see value in sponsoring reference genome projects, that could fund the creation of well-documented, verified profiles.
    • Over time, more institutions join, creating a large, credible repository.
  3. Legislative/Regulatory Pressure
    • If enough public demand arises (e.g., for unidentified remains or genealogical truth in lineage societies), lawmakers could require large DNA companies to provide an “open channel” for certain verified data sets.
    • That’s an unlikely scenario in the short term but could happen if enough momentum builds around the social benefits.
  4. Technological Convergence
    • As full-genome costs continue to drop, more people will have entire-genome data at home or from third-party labs.
    • The more such data accumulates outside the consumer DNA “walled gardens,” the more pressure there is to establish shared standards so people can do cross-platform genealogy or remain identification.

6. Conclusion

Your vision—an open, full-genome, global DNA reference system used by societies, law enforcement, and individuals—is technically achievable. The main challenges are:

  • Business inertia (consumer DNA companies lock down their pipelines).
  • Ethical/legal frameworks for how remains are tested and posted.
  • Financial feasibility and standardization efforts over the long haul.

Yet, in the grand scheme of 400-year (or more) institutions, it’s not far-fetched. If genealogical/historical societies, law enforcement, and nonprofits unite around an “open” approach—and if the public sees the social benefits—this could reshape how DNA data is shared, verified, and preserved for generations to come.
